articles.title: Minister backs legal right to job support for young people
articles.summary: The work and pensions secretary said the level of support currently on offer was too vague.
articles.content:
The work and pensions secretary has backed the idea that the government should legally guarantee young people help to get into employment.

Pat McFadden told the BBC that job support should be given a "legislative underpinning", adding the level of assistance on offer was currently "vague".

It comes ahead of a long-awaited review - set to be published on Tuesday - by former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn, which will say that under-25s should be guaranteed job placements or training to help them find permanent work.

Milburn is also expected to recommend that some young people should see their entitlement to claim benefits reduced, to free up funding for the new system.

Speaking to Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Milburn said he wanted a major shift in the ratio of spending on benefits versus employment support.

He has previously put this figure at about £25 is spent on benefits verses every £1 spent on employment support - a ratio he said he wants to see move to £2 to £1.

He added that there should be a new "duty on government" to provide young people with opportunities including apprenticeships, college places, job coaching, or a job.

This should be accompanied, he added, by "more obligations on their part to take up that opportunity".

Asked on the same programme whether he agreed with the idea, McFadden said: "I do think we need some legislative underpinning to this."

He added that the offer of support "needs to be more firm," adding: "People need more certainty about what they are entitled to."

It comes as the government announced it will further widen eligibly for its scheme that offers jobless under-25s subsidised six-month job roles on the minimum wage.

From next April, eligible claimants will be offered a role after 12 months of unsuccessfully looking for work, rather 18 currently.

It is the second time that eligibility for the scheme has been widened, after the maximum age was increased from 21 to 24 earlier this year.

It outlines concrete government commitments and planned reforms that aim to provide measurable benefits to youth employment, addressing a critical social issue with clear context and details.
articles.personality_title: Government moves to guarantee job support for young people by law
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Many young people struggle to find jobs after finishing school or college. Right now, the help they get from the government to find work is not clearly promised or strong enough.

**What happened** – The UK’s work and pensions secretary, Pat McFadden, said the government should make a legal promise to support young people in getting jobs. This means young people would be guaranteed help like apprenticeships, training, or job placements. A review by Alan Milburn, a former government minister, will soon suggest that under-25s should be guaranteed these opportunities. The government also plans to make more young people eligible for a scheme that gives them six-month paid jobs after a year of looking for work.

**Impact** – This is important because it makes job support clearer and more certain for young people. It could help many find permanent jobs faster and give them better chances to build their careers. The plan also aims to spend more money directly on helping people work, rather than just giving benefits without work support.

**What's next step** – The government will publish the full review soon and may change the law to guarantee this job support. They will also expand the job scheme starting next April, offering paid roles earlier to more young people who are unemployed.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The UK government is planning to legally guarantee young people support to find jobs, making help clearer and more reliable for those under 25.
articles.personality_title_fr: Le gouvernement prévoit de garantir légalement un soutien à l'emploi pour les jeunes
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Beaucoup de jeunes ont du mal à trouver un emploi après l'école ou les études. Actuellement, l'aide offerte par le gouvernement pour trouver du travail est floue et pas assez forte.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Pat McFadden, secrétaire au travail et aux pensions du Royaume-Uni, a déclaré que le gouvernement devrait promettre légalement de soutenir les jeunes dans leur recherche d'emploi. Cela signifie que les moins de 25 ans auraient la garantie d'avoir des aides comme des apprentissages, des formations ou des stages. Un rapport d'Alan Milburn, un ancien ministre, va bientôt recommander cette garantie. Le gouvernement prévoit aussi d'élargir un programme qui offre des emplois rémunérés de six mois aux jeunes au chômage après un an de recherche.

**Impact** – Cela rendra l'aide plus claire et certaine pour les jeunes. Cela pourrait les aider à trouver un emploi permanent plus rapidement et à mieux démarrer leur carrière. Le plan vise aussi à dépenser plus d'argent pour aider à travailler plutôt que seulement donner des aides sans accompagnement.

**Prochaine étape** – Le gouvernement publiera bientôt le rapport complet et pourrait changer la loi pour garantir ce soutien à l'emploi. Il élargira aussi le programme dès avril prochain, en offrant plus tôt des emplois rémunérés à davantage de jeunes sans emploi.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Le gouvernement britannique prévoit de garantir légalement un soutien à l'emploi pour les moins de 25 ans, rendant l'aide plus claire et fiable.
articles.personality_title_es: El gobierno planea garantizar legalmente el apoyo laboral para jóvenes
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Muchos jóvenes tienen dificultades para encontrar trabajo después de terminar la escuela o la universidad. Actualmente, la ayuda que ofrece el gobierno para encontrar empleo es vaga y no es suficiente.

**Qué pasó** – Pat McFadden, secretario de trabajo y pensiones del Reino Unido, dijo que el gobierno debería prometer por ley apoyar a los jóvenes para conseguir empleo. Esto significa que los menores de 25 años tendrían garantizada ayuda como aprendizajes, capacitación o colocaciones laborales. Una revisión de Alan Milburn, un exministro, sugerirá pronto que se garantice esta ayuda. El gobierno también planea ampliar un programa que ofrece trabajos pagados de seis meses a jóvenes desempleados después de un año buscando empleo.

**Impacto** – Esto es importante porque hace que el apoyo laboral sea más claro y seguro para los jóvenes. Podría ayudar a muchos a encontrar trabajos permanentes más rápido y a mejorar sus oportunidades para comenzar una carrera. El plan también busca gastar más dinero directamente en ayudar a las personas a trabajar, en lugar de solo dar beneficios sin apoyo laboral.

**Próximo paso** – El gobierno publicará la revisión completa pronto y podría cambiar la ley para garantizar este apoyo laboral. También ampliará el programa a partir de abril, ofreciendo roles pagados antes a más jóvenes desempleados.

**Resumen en una frase** – El gobierno del Reino Unido planea garantizar legalmente el apoyo laboral para jóvenes menores de 25 años, haciendo la ayuda más clara y confiable.

articles.title: How to shake hands and make eye contact: The lessons preparing pupils for the world of work
articles.summary: Year 10 pupils are learning employability skills to reduce the number of young people who end up "Neet".
articles.content:
There is a sudden buzz of conversation in a Year 10 class as teenagers split into pairs, sit down opposite each other and start conducting mock job interviews.

It is not for a forthcoming exam. These 14- and 15-year-olds at Sandbach High School and Sixth Form College are working on skills that should help them when they leave school and try to enter the workforce.

Today, they are learning the art of a successful job interview. Around the room, pupils are practising firm handshakes and making good eye contact.

They are rehearsing how to answer questions that you might expect to be asked in a job interview, such as "When was the last time you worked in a team?" and "Tell me about a time you made a mistake at work".

None of them has even reached working age yet, but in forthcoming lessons they'll also be learning about how to write a CV and what their rights at work are. It is all part of dedicated career lessons that they get every fortnight alongside their usual classes.

There are nearly a million young people across the UK - one in eight of all those aged 16 to 24 - who are not in education, employment or training - or Neet - according to the latest estimates.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has called the high number both a "moral failure" and an "economic catastrophe".
articles.reasoning: The article describes a practical educational initiative aimed at equipping young people with employability skills to reduce the number of youth not in education, employment, or training (NEET). This has a meaningful societal impact by addressing youth unemployment and improving future opportunities for a significant demographic, with clear context and focus on the program's benefits.
articles.personality_title: Year 10 pupils learn job skills to prepare for work life
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Many young people in the UK, about one in eight aged 16 to 24, are not in education, employment, or training. This group is often called NEET. Being NEET can make it harder for young people to find good jobs later.

**What happened** – At Sandbach High School and Sixth Form College, Year 10 students aged 14 and 15 are taking special lessons to build job skills. They practice things like shaking hands firmly, making eye contact, and answering common interview questions. They also learn how to write CVs and understand their rights at work.

**Impact** – These lessons give students a chance to prepare for real job interviews before they even leave school. Practicing these skills early helps them feel more confident and ready for work or training. This approach aims to reduce the number of young people becoming NEET by giving them practical tools to succeed.

**What's next step** – The school will continue teaching these career lessons every two weeks. If this program works well, other schools might adopt similar lessons to help more young people across the UK get ready for work.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Teaching job skills to 14- and 15-year-olds helps prepare them for future work and can lower youth unemployment risks.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les élèves de 4e apprennent des compétences pour réussir dans le monde du travail
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Au Royaume-Uni, environ un jeune sur huit âgé de 16 à 24 ans n’est ni en formation, ni en emploi, ni en éducation. On appelle ce groupe les NEET. Être NEET complique souvent la recherche d’un bon emploi plus tard.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Au Sandbach High School and Sixth Form College, des élèves de 4e (14-15 ans) suivent des cours spéciaux pour acquérir des compétences professionnelles. Ils s’exercent à serrer la main fermement, à regarder les gens dans les yeux et à répondre aux questions d’entretien. Ils apprennent aussi à rédiger un CV et à connaître leurs droits au travail.

**Impact** – Ces cours donnent aux élèves l’occasion de se préparer aux vrais entretiens d’embauche avant de quitter l’école. S’exercer à ces compétences tôt les aide à être plus confiants et prêts pour le travail ou la formation. Cette méthode vise à réduire le nombre de jeunes NEET en leur donnant des outils pratiques.

**Prochaine étape** – L’école continuera ces cours de carrière toutes les deux semaines. Si ce programme réussit, d’autres écoles pourraient adopter des leçons similaires pour aider plus de jeunes à travers le Royaume-Uni.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Apprendre des compétences professionnelles aux jeunes de 14-15 ans les prépare au travail futur et peut réduire les risques de chômage chez les jeunes.
articles.personality_title_es: Alumnos de 4º de ESO aprenden habilidades para el mundo laboral
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En el Reino Unido, aproximadamente uno de cada ocho jóvenes de 16 a 24 años no está estudiando, trabajando ni en formación. A este grupo se le llama NEET. Ser NEET dificulta encontrar buenos empleos en el futuro.

**Qué pasó** – En Sandbach High School and Sixth Form College, los alumnos de 4º de ESO (14 y 15 años) reciben clases especiales para aprender habilidades laborales. Practican dar un apretón de manos firme, hacer contacto visual y responder preguntas comunes en entrevistas de trabajo. También aprenden a redactar currículums y a conocer sus derechos laborales.

**Impacto** – Estas lecciones permiten a los estudiantes prepararse para entrevistas reales antes de salir de la escuela. Practicar estas habilidades temprano les ayuda a sentirse más seguros y listos para trabajar o formarse. Este método busca reducir el número de jóvenes NEET dándoles herramientas prácticas.

**Próximo paso** – La escuela seguirá impartiendo estas clases de carrera cada dos semanas. Si el programa funciona, otras escuelas podrían usar lecciones similares para ayudar a más jóvenes en todo el Reino Unido.

**Resumen en una frase** – Enseñar habilidades laborales a jóvenes de 14 y 15 años los prepara para el trabajo futuro y puede disminuir el desempleo juvenil.
